title: Explaining a dual value to a finance partner

questions.stem: A utility's LP writes its line-crew row in $k of crew capacity, and that row's price is 0.15 ($k of NPV per $k of capacity). One crew-week delivers $200k of work. A contractor offers one crew-week for $25k, paid from outside the capital budget, and the extra capacity stays inside the row's range. What should the planner conclude?

options.text: Hire: a crew-week adds $30k of value against a cost of $25k
options.says: Right: convert the unit first, 0.15 per $k of capacity times 200 $k per crew-week is 30 per crew-week.

options.text: Pass: a crew-week adds $0.15k of value against a cost of $25k
options.says: 0.15 is per $k of capacity, not per crew-week; multiply by the $k one crew-week delivers.

options.text: Hire: a crew-week adds $200k of value against a cost of $25k
options.says: 200 is the work a crew-week delivers, not its value; the value is the price times that work.

options.text: Pass: a crew-week adds $3.75k of value against a cost of $25k
options.says: Multiplying the price by the contractor's cost mixes units; multiply it by the capacity a crew-week adds.

origin.section: Say a Price's Unit, Its Direction and Its Range

questions.stem: A maximization LP has a regulatory minimum: inspect at least 600 km of line. At the optimum its price is -0.2 per km. A manager concludes that the rule costs the plan 120 (600 times 0.2). What is right?

options.text: It costs exactly 120, since the price applies to every km of the rule
options.says: A price is marginal: it prices the last km. The vegetation floor priced at -0.12 x 900 = 108 really cost 100.2.

options.text: It costs nothing, since the minimum is met by the optimal plan
options.says: A binding requirement with a nonzero price does cost value; its price is the cost of one more unit.

options.text: Its total needs a re-solve without it, since 0.2 prices only the last km
options.says: Right: the total cost of a commitment is the value without it minus the value with it.

options.text: It earns 120, since a negative price means the plan gains from it
options.says: A negative price on a minimum means raising it lowers the value: the rule costs, it does not earn.

origin.section: A Negative Price Is the Marginal Cost of a Commitment

questions.stem: A capital-planning model chooses yes/no projects with binary variables and is solved as a MILP. The board asks what an extra $1M of budget would be worth. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Read the budget row's dual value from MathOpt and scale it to $1M
options.says: MathOpt has no dual values for a MILP; asking for them raises an error.

options.text: Re-solve the MILP with the larger budget and report the change in value
options.says: Right: a MILP's value moves in steps, so the answer is a scenario re-solve.

options.text: Use the LP relaxation's budget price, since it is the MILP's slope too
options.says: The relaxation's price prices fractions of projects; the MILP's value rose by 123 and then by 0 per $100k where the LP's price stayed 0.4929.

options.text: Report zero, since a yes/no model's value cannot change with budget
options.says: It can change, in steps: the selection model gained 123 between budgets of 7,000 and 7,100.

origin.section: A Yes/No Model Has No Shadow Prices, Only Re-Solves
